overview: Peninsular Nova Scotia became a British colonial territory within Mi’kma’ki, the homeland of the Mi’kmaq. Its history includes Acadian farming, forced displacement, port towns and diverse migrant communities. The peninsula shown by this map record belongs to Nova Scotia; the colony’s larger boundaries changed over time.

periods.title: British rule over an Acadian landscape
periods.summary: The Treaty of Utrecht transferred French claims to peninsular Acadia to Britain in 1713. Mi’kmaq communities and Acadian settlements remained part of the region’s history; the treaty did not make the peninsula an empty territory.

periods.title: Deportation and new settlement
periods.summary: The 1755 Acadian deportation transformed communities such as Grand-Pré. New England Planters later settled there and adopted the existing marshland farming system.

periods.title: Loyalist arrival and unequal opportunity
periods.summary: Black Loyalists arrived after the American Revolution and built communities, including Birchtown. Freedom did not bring equal access to land, wages or provisions.

periods.title: Continuing communities and colonial change
periods.summary: Some Black Loyalists emigrated to Sierra Leone in 1792, while many remained. Communities continued to earn livelihoods in fisheries, skilled trades, farming and other work.

periods.title: A province in the Canadian federation
periods.summary: Nova Scotia joined the Canadian federation in 1867. Confederation changed its political position within British North America; Canada’s independence from Britain developed through later steps.

items.text: Acadian dykes used wooden sluices called aboiteaux. At low tide, freshwater drained outward; rising seawater pushed a valve shut. Rain and melting snow gradually removed salt from the enclosed ground, allowing cultivation. The system adapted earlier techniques to the Bay of Fundy’s demanding tidal environment.

Wheat, oats and flax grew on reclaimed land. Roads could run along dyke tops, with oxen or horses pulling carts. Water management therefore shaped both food production and everyday movement, while continued maintenance was essential to protecting the fields.

At Melanson, rectangular depressions and grassy mounds preserve traces interpreted as collapsed chimneys or ovens. Circular mounds may mark wells, mills and other structures. Eighteenth-century engineers’ plans help researchers connect these features to a family-based settlement, while some individual functions remain uncertain.

After deportation, Planter settlement overlaid the Acadian landscape at Grand-Pré. The newcomers used its established drainage technology. Continuity of farmland must therefore be distinguished from continuity of ownership or an absence of forced displacement.

Excavation of the late eighteenth-century site AkDi 12 revealed a cellar-like feature. Initially interpreted as a root cellar, it was later understood as a temporary dwelling used around the first winter of Black Loyalist settlement in 1783. That interpretation links household remains to the difficulties of establishing shelter.

At AkDi 23, archaeologists recovered ceramics, matched dish sets, military buttons, a bayonet and a boarding axe. They associated the assemblage with Stephen Blucke’s property on the basis of its character and quality. The attribution is an archaeological argument, not proof supplied by the objects alone.

Birchtown residents worked in fishing, woodcutting, land clearing, domestic service and day labour. Black settlers received smaller grants and provisions, or none, and faced lower wages. Meanwhile, some white Loyalists brought enslaved people, so freedom and slavery coexisted in colonial Nova Scotia.

The 1792 emigrants carried tools, furniture, muskets and spinning wheels to Sierra Leone. Such belongings show the practical resources families valued when moving again. Other community members, including teachers and ship pilots, remained in Nova Scotia.

sections.title: A waterfront town and its carpentry

items.text: Lunenburg was laid out in 1753 on a rectangular street grid. Its surviving wooden houses and public buildings, property divisions and working waterfront preserve the organisation of a colonial town whose economy was closely tied to offshore fishing. The plan and the buildings are related evidence of urban life.

Benjamin Knaut’s house, built in 1793 to 1794, combined a New England Colonial exterior with a Georgian interior plan. It belonged to a substantial estate with gardens and an orchard. As a merchant’s home, it records wealth and skilled building, not the housing conditions of every resident.

Conrad Rhuland, a mariner and privateer, bought the house in 1813 and changed its front parlour in a regional German vernacular style. The building’s successive alterations show how residents adapted inherited structures rather than preserving a single untouched colonial moment.

The Mi’kmawey Debert Cultural Centre explains the Peace and Friendship Treaties as reciprocal agreements involving trade, settlement and distinct legal authorities. They did not surrender Mi’kmaq territory. Colonial control on a map must therefore not be read as a treaty cession of Indigenous land.

In 1784, New Brunswick and Cape Breton became separate colonies from Nova Scotia; Cape Breton rejoined it in 1820. These administrative changes explain why a map of the peninsula cannot stand for the whole colony at every date.

ending.text: Nova Scotia entered the Canadian federation in 1867 as a province. This was a constitutional transformation, not a military fall or the disappearance of its communities. Confederation also did not immediately end Canada’s relationship of dependence on Britain. The map’s 1815 endpoint is only the end of this imported label’s coverage.
